references.note: OSNI Baronies and Parishes maps obtained via FOI request to Mapping.Helpdesk@finance-ni.gov.uk, who commented as follows: "The Parish and Baronies dataset was created in 2007 based on the existing Townlands dataset combined with NISRA data for a specific project. While it was originally envisaged that the dataset would be released as an additional OSNI product for public supply, it proved difficult to verify the exact townlands making up parishes due to conflicts within source material. The data was developed to a state that was fit-for-purpose at the time, however, OSNI was unable to fully QA the product and so was not considered to be at a sufficient standard to add to our product catalogue. As customers enquired after the dataset, as a goodwill gesture, we agreed to share it on request, with the understanding that it is not an official product and so we could not stand over its accuracy or completeness. For the same reason, there is no documentation or analysis of the data to support it. Therefore, the only additional information we can provide you with is what we have observed from our own review of the data: there are topographical errors, such as sliver polygons, missing attribution and additional fields that could be cleansed out if desired."

references.label: Civil Parishes of Ireland -- OSNI provenance
references.note: OSNI Baronies and Parishes maps obtained via FOI request to Mapping.Helpdesk@finance-ni.gov.uk, who commented as follows: "The Parish and Baronies dataset was created in 2007 based on the existing Townlands dataset combined with NISRA data for a specific project. While it was originally envisaged that the dataset would be released as an additional OSNI product for public supply, it proved difficult to verify the exact townlands making up parishes due to conflicts within source material. The data was developed to a state that was fit-for-purpose at the time, however, OSNI was unable to fully QA the product and so was not considered to be at a sufficient standard to add to our product catalogue. As customers enquired after the dataset, as a goodwill gesture, we agreed to share it on request, with the understanding that it is not an official product and so we could not stand over its accuracy or completeness. For the same reason, there is no documentation or analysis of the data to support it. Therefore, the only additional information we can provide you with is what we have observed from our own review of the data: there are topographical errors, such as sliver polygons, missing attribution and additional fields that could be cleansed out if desired."

Description: Abstract cube sculpture.
Commissioned as part of the Per Cent for Art Scheme, this is a series of colourful, locally inspired images in bronze and mosaic panels, inset into the pavement along the main street.

Commissioned by Harbour Company.  The artwork is in recognition of the perilous work the Hobbling Community once performed in guiding incoming vessels safely into the port of Dún Laoghaire and assisting mooring right up to the 1930’s.
Commissioned by Harbour Company. A sculpture of stylised boat sails.
Commissioned by Harbour Company. A sinuous mosaic seat.

Dedicated to the memory of painter Cecil King, this piece was erected specifically to be interactive for young children. The geometric form in red painted steel stands monumental and proud against a mid-ground of the surrounding greenery.

Dreaming about The Celestial Mountain is about journeys that will never be made except in the imagination. The path to the summit forms a labyrinth, and steps are inscribed with a poem that describes the preparations required for a successful journey.

Eclipse stands directly on grass, appearing to defy gravity by not rolling over to allow the heavy element at the top to rest. The sculpture is cylindrical in form, standing upright with a thinner tube form emerging from its side on the same plane.

Originally sited in Marlay Park, Archer II was designed with children in mind. The work deals with the tension and release of energy and specifically expresses a momentary release of energy; frozen time, petrified, solidified.

The Usher Monument was erected to the memory of the late Dr. Isaac Usher. It takes the form of a granite fountain with four baths designed to collect water from cast iron fittings. The pillar is ribbed delicately and takes the form of an obelisk.
These brightly coloured mosaic trees are sited on a wall in Carriglea Gardens estate.  The work was created using a variety of ceramic tiles in a broad spectrum of cheerful colours.

This cast bronze and stainless steel piece depicts a sea urchin positioned on its side as if suspended in motion leaving a trail of metal silver droplets. It is as if the sea urchin has been thrown up onto the shore by a wave.

This monument pays tribute to King George IV and the renaming of Dunleary. It also records the laying of the first stone of the harbour in 1817. The base is a huge mound of granite upon which sits four large granite spheres, holding up the monument pillar.

This monumental piece stands at the entrance to Cromlech Fields housing estate. It is made from two large pieces of granite with a bronze section connecting them and is reminiscent of dolmens acting as a gateway to the estate.

This piece was commissioned at the behest of the bicycle shopkeeper in Dundrum who supplied parts and gave encouragement to the young Stephen Roche. The bronze design represents bicycle gears, the lettered granite circle the movement of the cycle wheels.
This sculpture, commissioned by renowned artist Thomas Glendon, honours those who died in the Rising and are buried at Deansgrange Cemetery.
This tapering pillar carved with woodland motifs represents the fringes of the woods in early summer, beautifully resembling a bird bath.

This work consists of four separate bronze discs, representing an eclipse, sited on four different walls in the housing development. The work is set into the fabric of the wall at a height and each piece is surrounded by brickwork detail.
This work consists of two sunflowers carved in relief in limestone and sited beside each other. The piece is mounted on a wall making the artworks appear like two stone pictures.

This work was commissioned for the residents of the three purpose-built homes for senior citizens at Ard Lorcan Villas. It is wall-mounted and based upon the structure of a crossword. The selection of words was chosen to help create a welcoming atmosphere.

layers.name: District Electoral Divisions/Wards 1971
layers.description: Republic of Ireland District Electoral Divisions/Wards as at 1971-04-15, assembled from Connacht (= 1957 boundaries), Leinster 1971, Munster 1971, Ulster (= 1963 boundaries). Modified version of District Electoral Divisions/Wards 1977. In 1977, due to the expansion of Drogheda, part of the DED of St. Mary’s was ceded to County Louth by County Meath. Details on this can be found in the Local Government Provisional Order Confirmation Act, 1976. Also relevant is the renaming of An Uaimh to Navan on 25/06/1971, as its corresponding DEDs were renamed by 1971 Census Reports Volume 1 (published July 1972).

layers.name: District Electoral Divisions/Wards 1980
layers.description: Republic of Ireland District Electoral Divisions/Wards as at 1980-01-01, assembled from Connacht (= 1957 boundaries), Leinster (= 1977 boundaries), Munster 1980, Ulster (= 1963 boundaries). layers.description: Republic of Ireland District Electoral Divisions/Wards as at 1994, assembled from Connacht (= 1986 boundaries), Leinster 1994, Munster (= 1983 boundaries), Ulster (= 1963 boundaries). The difference between this and that map is that the electoral division of Cherry Orchard B was renamed to Carna (source used - County Borough of Dublin (Wards) (Amendment) Regulations, 1997). District electoral divisions and wards were both renamed to electoral divisions in 1996 via the Local Government Act 1994, hence the new "WARDORDED" attribute

Site_Descr: A change in NATO policy in the 1970s changed tripwire defence against the Warsaw Pact to that of ‘flexible response’, whereby aggression by the Soviet Union would be met by a proportional response rather than nuclear retaliation as a first option. Th
A complex of dog kennels used to house dog security element for radar station.
A large workshop for maintaining the onsite radar equipment. It is attached by a corridor to the administration block

Aircraft were refuelled using mobile tankers, which were refilled from the bulk storage sites. An operational airfield was required to maintain six weeks of fuel. Therefore, Bishops Court had a single 72,000 gallon bulk storage installation for aviation

Aircraft were refuelled using mobile tankers, which were refilled from the bulk storage sites. Pumps would have serviced the fuel tankers which parked on the circular hard-standing. This site does not appear on WW2 maps therefore it was added post war an

Blister hangars were small arched dispersal shed, made of wood or welded steel, and were used for the maintenance and storage of aircraft with small wingspans. They were clad in steel sheeting and had quick-release canvas curtains on either end.

Blister hangars were small arched dispersal sheds, made of wood or welded steel, and were used for the maintenance and storage of aircraft with small wingspans. They were clad in steel sheeting and had quick-release canvas curtains on either end.

By 1942 the huge increase in aircraft numbers made the use of ‘frying pan’ dispersals unworkable. Consequently, the dispersals were redesigned into ‘spectacle’ or loop dispersals sited around the perimeter track. They had many advantages over the
Communications tower used to maintain communications with Army HQ at Thiepval Barracks, Lisburn.
Contained boilers and fuel store for heating system, providing heat to nearby barracks
Described as a line terminal building on RAF map, clearly a technical building housing electronic equipment, exact function remains unclear.

Known as a technical latrine, it was used by ground crew who were working in the store, workshops or on aircraft. Often divided into sections of officers and other ranks.
Landing pad for helicopters flown into site. The helipad provides a clearly marked hard surface away from obstacles where such aircraft can land safely.
Large (4x4m) concrete and steel blocks used to support a crane, likely used to install the Type 84 radar on the modulator building.
Latrine providing toilet facilities for female (WAAF) personnel
Nissen hut housing Rooms for pilots and ground crew while working at aircraft on dispersals/ blister hangers.
Office accommodation for the administration of the attached motor transport unit
Office for clerks and timekeepers, housed in Nissen hut.

Overall the airfield remains in remarkable state of preservation, with many of the structures remaining from World War 2 and the Cold War era of its occupation. Much of the runway and perimeter track survives in good condition. Construction of the Bishop
Plinth for a Type 13 height finding radar, which provided height information on aircraft using centimentric radar. The transmitting equipment was housed inside the plinth .
Provided accommodation for airmen. Built on site of WW2 huts.

In good condition, some grass growing through expansion joints.

In good condition, used as crew/pit area for race circuit.

layers.name: North Coast Post-Storm Survey LiDAR — March 2022 (3D)
layers.description: Airborne LiDAR point cloud of the Causeway Coast, flown March 2022 as a post-storm survey in the DAERA NI 3D Coastal Survey programme, elevation-shaded. Recovered from the published ArcGIS i3s scene layer and streamed in 3D as an OGC 3D-Tiles octree via deck.gl: tilt and zoom in and the individual scanned points load in place; zoom out and they unload. Pairs with the September 2022 recovery survey for before/after comparison. (One central section of the corridor is omitted where the source scene layer could not be read.)

layers.name: OSNI Historical Six-Inch Maps — Edition 1 (1829–1835)
layers.description: The original Six-Inch-to-One-Mile County Series — the first complete topographic survey of Ireland, produced 1829–1835 by the Ordnance Survey. 308 historical map sheets covering all six Northern Ireland counties (Antrim, Armagh, Derry/Londonderry, Down, Fermanagh, Tyrone), engraved at a scale where every individual building, road, field boundary, and town feature is shown. Mosaicked and re-tiled here at 4 m/pixel for interactive viewing on the catalogue map. For pixel-level detail, download the original sheet TIFs from the per-county packages linked below.

layers.name: OSNI Historical Six-Inch Maps — Edition 2 (1838–1862)
layers.description: Second edition of the Six-Inch-to-One-Mile County Series, surveyed 1838–1862, providing the first comprehensive update to the original 1830s survey. 261 historical sheets covering all six Northern Ireland counties. Captures the rapid changes in Irish landscape, settlement patterns, and infrastructure during the mid-19th century — including the period before, during, and immediately after the Great Famine (1845–1852). Mosaicked and re-tiled here at 4 m/pixel.

layers.name: Tellus Electromagnetic — 14 kHz Apparent Conductivity
layers.description: Apparent ground conductivity at 14 kHz — shallower depth (~10–30 m) than the 3 kHz channel, more sensitive to surface and near-surface conductors. Useful for soil moisture, near-surface alteration, and thin clay layers. Viridis colormap, -2σ to +4σ stretch.

references.label: OSNI Open Data — Tellus Electromagnetic Grids

layers.notes: Raster XYZ tile layer using metadata bounds and tile template https://data.civgraph.net/data/maps/geology/tellus-em-14khz/{z}/{x}/{y}.png.

layers.name: Tellus Electromagnetic — 3 kHz Apparent Conductivity
layers.description: Apparent ground conductivity at 3 kHz from the Tellus airborne EM survey — penetrates ~50–150 m, mapping conductive saline groundwater, clay-rich soils, mineralised zones, and pollution plumes. Viridis colormap (low = purple, high = yellow), -2σ to +4σ stretch.

references.label: OSNI Open Data — Tellus Electromagnetic Grids

layers.notes: Raster XYZ tile layer using metadata bounds and tile template https://data.civgraph.net/data/maps/geology/tellus-em-3khz/{z}/{x}/{y}.png.

layers.name: Tellus Airborne Survey — Flight Lines
layers.description: The actual flight-line pattern flown by the Tellus airborne geophysical survey (2005–2008) — 2 210 individual flight lines at ~250 m spacing across all of Northern Ireland, derived from the raw radiometric sample positions. Toggle on alongside any of the gridded magnetic / electromagnetic / radiometric layers to see where the survey actually sampled the ground; anomalies on the gridded products are most reliable inside dense flight coverage and progressively less reliable on the edges and in gaps. Single inert MultiLineString — non-interactive (no per-line popup, hover, or click) so it doesn't compete with the per-feature data layers underneath.

references.label: OSNI Open Data — Tellus Radiometrics raw (source)

layers.notes: Generated from render/source-cache/vector-intake/tellus-flight-tracks.fgb with GDAL MVT output.

layers.name: Tellus Magnetic — Reduction-to-Pole (RTP)
layers.description: TMI corrected by reduction-to-pole, which compensates for the dipolar shape of magnetic anomalies caused by NI's inclined magnetic field. RTP places the peak directly above the source body, simplifying interpretation. ±3σ rainbow ramp.

references.label: OSNI Open Data — Tellus Magnetic Grids

layers.notes: Raster XYZ tile layer using metadata bounds and tile template https://data.civgraph.net/data/maps/geology/tellus-mag-rtp/{z}/{x}/{y}.png.

layers.name: Tellus Magnetic — RTP Tilt Derivative
layers.description: Tilt derivative of the RTP magnetic field — an edge-detection filter that highlights the boundaries of magnetic source bodies regardless of their amplitude. Excellent for tracing dykes, faults, and contacts. ±3σ rainbow ramp.

references.label: OSNI Open Data — Tellus Magnetic Grids

layers.notes: Raster XYZ tile layer using metadata bounds and tile template https://data.civgraph.net/data/maps/geology/tellus-mag-rtp-tilt/{z}/{x}/{y}.png.

layers.name: Tellus Magnetic — Total Magnetic Intensity (residual)
layers.description: Residual total magnetic intensity (TMI) from the GSNI Tellus airborne survey — variations in the Earth's magnetic field caused by buried magnetic minerals (chiefly magnetite). High-magnetic anomalies trace mafic/ultramafic intrusions, basaltic flows, and iron-bearing sedimentary basins; magnetic lows mark sedimentary basins and demagnetised alteration zones. 35m grid spacing, ±3σ rainbow ramp.

references.label: OSNI Open Data — Tellus Magnetic Grids

layers.notes: Raster XYZ tile layer using metadata bounds and tile template https://data.civgraph.net/data/maps/geology/tellus-mag-tmi/{z}/{x}/{y}.png.

layers.name: Tellus Radiometric — Potassium (K %)
layers.description: Surface potassium concentration from natural gamma-ray emissions. Highlights granites and other felsic intrusions (potassium-rich), alkaline volcanics, and certain sedimentary horizons. Inferno colormap (dark = low, bright = high), ±2-3σ stretch.

references.label: OSNI Open Data — Tellus Radiometric Grids

layers.notes: Raster XYZ tile layer using metadata bounds and tile template https://data.civgraph.net/data/maps/geology/tellus-rad-k/{z}/{x}/{y}.png.

layers.name: Tellus Radiometric — K/Th/U Ternary RGB
layers.description: The iconic radiometric ternary composite — K mapped to red, Th to green, U to blue. Reds = potassic (granite, certain volcanics); greens = thorium-rich (resistate sediments, heavy minerals); blues = uranium-rich (organic shales, mineralisation); whites/pale = high in all three; blacks = low overall. The most interpretively powerful single radiometric view. Each band stretched independently to mean ± 2σ.

references.label: OSNI Open Data — Tellus Radiometric Grids

layers.notes: Raster XYZ tile layer using metadata bounds and tile template https://data.civgraph.net/data/maps/geology/tellus-rad-ternary/{z}/{x}/{y}.png.

layers.name: Tellus Radiometric — Thorium-Equivalent (eTh ppm)
layers.description: Thorium-equivalent concentration from the 2.61 MeV thallium-208 daughter peak. Often correlates with heavy minerals (monazite, zircon) in placer deposits and resistate sediments. Rainbow colormap, ±2-3σ stretch.

references.label: OSNI Open Data — Tellus Radiometric Grids

layers.notes: Raster XYZ tile layer using metadata bounds and tile template https://data.civgraph.net/data/maps/geology/tellus-rad-th/{z}/{x}/{y}.png.

layers.name: Tellus Radiometric — Total Counts (gamma)
layers.description: Total gamma-ray count rate — a summed proxy for combined K, U, Th, and other radionuclide activity. Useful for identifying overall radiometric "hot" zones before decomposing into individual channels. Inferno colormap, ±2-3σ stretch.

references.label: OSNI Open Data — Tellus Radiometric Grids

layers.notes: Raster XYZ tile layer using metadata bounds and tile template https://data.civgraph.net/data/maps/geology/tellus-rad-total/{z}/{x}/{y}.png.

layers.name: Tellus Radiometric — Uranium-Equivalent (eU ppm)
layers.description: Uranium-equivalent concentration from the 1.76 MeV bismuth-214 daughter peak. Highlights uranium-bearing granites, organic-rich shales, phosphatic horizons, and mineralised zones. Viridis colormap, ±2-3σ stretch.

references.label: OSNI Open Data — Tellus Radiometric Grids

layers.notes: Raster XYZ tile layer using metadata bounds and tile template https://data.civgraph.net/data/maps/geology/tellus-rad-u/{z}/{x}/{y}.png.

layers.name: DAERA Network Contribution — SciMAP modelled pollution scores by river basin (26 catchments)
layers.description: Per-river-basin pollution-contribution scores from the SciMAP hydrological model (CEH Land Cover 2007 + Met Office rainfall + 5 m DTM), rasterised at 25 m and rendered as a Web Mercator tile pyramid coloured on inferno (low → high contribution). Raw GRIDCODE values of 58–100 stretch the inferno ramp from dark purple to pale yellow. Each parcel of land is scored for how much sediment / nutrient pollution its upstream catchment contributes to receiving waters. 26 catchment datasets were rasterised individually, mosaicked, and re-projected; per-catchment download links remain in sourceDownloads for the raw vector data.

layers.name: District Electoral Divisions 3 May 1921
layers.description: Northern Ireland District Electoral Divisions as at 3 May 1921. A modified version of the 1911 DEDs/wards map, capturing the three changes made in the six counties between 1911 and partition: the DED of Gortahurk ceded six townlands to Cuilcagh (both in Fermanagh), and Portstewart and Ballycastle each split their DED into urban and rural.
